To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the transition towards co-ownership of Bosland is a process that has been initiated by an active group of stakeholders that are willing to experiment and take risks.
the Bosland model of forest management is a co-ownership model that is characterized by a long-term vision, a bottom up approach, and management for coherence.

Bosland is a pioneering case in which a new way of forest management is adopted, geared towards management for multiple ecosystem services, where a long term vision guides short term action, and where a bottom up approach focusing upon participation is adopted to co-create the management agenda.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how a new forest management approach can emerge and be sustained in a complex and contested socio-ecological system.
the emergence of new ways of managing forests, which are more oriented towards sustainability and multifunctionality and which are co-owned by multiple stakeholders.
the question of how a pioneering co-owned forest management model can be understood and what are its key features.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Bosland is not a transition but a case of a transition trajectory.
Bosland is a case of transition, but not yet of transformation.
Bosland is an example of a pioneering case of a transition in forest management towards co-ownership.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Bosland model is an example for a transition towards a new way of managing forest for coherence.
a change in forest management is not only possible, but also that a new way of forest management is already being implemented and can be successful, if the key features are present.
Bosland has evolved towards a more integrated, participatory and long-term approach to forest management.
The main takeaway from our work is that

a change in forest management can be achieved by a combination of bottom up and top down initiatives and that the use of a transition framework is helpful in identifying and understanding the key features of such a change trajectory.
Bosland can serve as a model for other regions in Western-Europe to learn from and to build on.

Bosland is a pioneering case of forest management where a more integrated, coherent and participatory way of managing is developed, and which can serve as a blueprint for future co-owned forest management.
